To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) fire exclusion coupled with infrequent active management activities contributed significantly to trends in departure from historic reference conditions in the ponderosa pine ecosystems of the Kaibab National Forest in northern Arizona; 2) the ecological departure rating for current conditions is high (0.85), and is expected to increase in the future; 3) the ecological departure ratings are sensitive to assumptions about fire frequency and fire severity; and 4) climate change is likely to exacerbate trends in ecological departure from
the contemporary model of the ponderosa pine ecosystem of the Kaibab National Forest is not sustainable in the long term.
fire suppression coupled by infrequent management activities has contributed to a departure from reference conditions in the study area.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the sustainability of fire-adaptive ecosystems in the face of changing environmental conditions and management regimes.
developing an ecological sustainability framework to evaluate management practices that affect forest ecosystems.
the development of a process for evaluating the ecological sustainability of ponderosa pine ecosystems, and for identifying the ecological and social tradeoffs of alternative management strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ponderosa pine ecosystem on the Kaibaba Plateau in northern Arizona is in a state of ecological departure, but that it is still possible to reverse this trend.
the ecological sustainability of the ecosystem is not being maintained.
the current management practices are not sustainable in the long run.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach to evaluating ecological sustainability is a useful tool for assessing current conditions and for projecting the effects of current and alternative management scenarios.
the current management regime is unsustainable.

the current management of ponderosa pine forests in northern Arizona has contributed to significant departures in ecological sustainability, and that the current management paradigm will not be able to sustain these ecosystems in the future.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be able to describe the ecological sustainability of a forest ecosystem in a way that can be communicated to a wide audience, including managers and policy makers.
the VDDT can be a useful tool for assessing the effects of management activities on the sustainability of ecosystems.
the process we developed can be applied to other systems, and that the process can be used to evaluate the sustainability of management activities.
